readerTitle: Better and cheaper, yet still losing: what customers really pay for
caseNote: 가상 사례 2개 (동네 비스트로, 프리랜서용 청구서 앱) + 실제 연구 (Sheth·Newman·Gross 1991, Bain & Company 2016)
insight: 고객은 제품이 '하는 일'만 사지 않는다. 그것이 주는 느낌과 남에게 보이는 모습까지 함께 산다. 경쟁에서 지는 이유가 기능이 아닐 때가 많다.
misconception: 제품이 더 좋고 더 싸면 고객은 당연히 우리를 고른다. 지고 있다면 기능이나 가격이 부족한 것이다.

sources.text: Sheth, J. N., Newman, B. I., & Gross, B. L. (1991). Why we buy what we buy: A theory of consumption values. Journal of Business Research, 22(2), 159–170.
Almquist, E., Senior, J., & Bloch, N. (2016). The Elements of Value. Harvard Business Review, September 2016.
비스트로와 청구서 앱 사례는 설명용 가상 사례

factChecks.note: Sheth·Newman·Gross(1991)는 소비 가치를 functional, social, emotional, epistemic, conditional 다섯 가지로 제시했습니다. 카드에는 '세 가지를 포함한 여러 가치'로만 적었습니다. 서지 정보(권·호·쪽)를 게시 전 다시 확인하세요.
Bain의 Elements of Value는 30개 요소를 functional, emotional, life changing, social impact 네 층의 피라미드로 묶었습니다. 요소 수와 층 이름, HBR 게재 호(2016년 9월)를 다시 확인하세요. 성과 관련 수치는 카드에 쓰지 않았습니다.
비스트로와 청구서 앱의 상황, 고객 반응은 모두 가상입니다. 수치는 쓰지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Better and cheaper, yet still losing
body: A neighborhood bistro has better reviews and lower prices than the place across town. An invoicing app is faster and cheaper than the market leader.
Both keep losing customers to the pricier rival. Neither has a quality problem. They have the same blind spot.

image.label: A cozy bistro and a laptop invoice, each losing to a pricier rival
image.brief: 화면을 좌우로 나눈 일러스트. 왼쪽은 따뜻한 동네 비스트로, 오른쪽은 노트북 화면 속 청구서. 양쪽 모두 손님/사용자 실루엣이 화살표를 따라 더 비싼 경쟁자 쪽으로 걸어감. 실제 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Regulars love you, but not for birthdays.
body: You run the bistro. Regulars come for weeknight dinners and praise the food. But for birthdays and anniversaries, they book the pricier place across town.
What do you change first?

options.text: Cut weekend prices to win those bookings
options.feedback: You give up margin to fix a gap that isn't about price. People already pay more across town on purpose.

options.text: Add premium dishes so the menu feels more special
options.feedback: Better food helps a little, but food was never the weak spot. You'd spend on the thing you already win.

options.text: Design for the occasion: quiet tables, a personal note, staff who mark the moment
options.feedback: This targets what the rival actually sells on those nights. It costs some staff time and attention, not a price cut.

cards.title: The rival wasn't selling better food.
body: On a Tuesday, a customer wants a good meal close to home. The bistro wins.
On an anniversary, the same customer wants more. They want the evening to *feel* like an event. And they want their partner to see that they made an effort.
The place across town delivers both. The bistro only delivers the meal.

cards.title: Three kinds of value
body: **Functional value** is what a product does: feeds you, saves time, sends the invoice.
**Emotional value** is how it makes the customer feel: calm, celebrated, in control. **Social value** is how it makes them look to others, or the group it lets them belong to.
Most purchases carry all three. What changes is the mix, and the mix can shift for the same customer from one day to the next.

image.label: Three stacked layers labeled Does, Feels, Signals
image.brief: 쟁반 위 저녁 한 접시를 세 겹 층으로 표현한 인포그래픽. 아래층 "Does: a good meal", 가운데 "Feels: celebrated", 위층 "Signals: I made an effort". 위 두 층이 반투명하게 빛나도록.

cards.title: One anniversary dinner, three jobs
body: The bistro wins the bottom row. The rival wins the two rows above it, and those decide the booking.

breakdown.label: Functional
breakdown.detail: A good meal, nearby, fairly priced. The bistro wins.

breakdown.label: Emotional
breakdown.detail: The night feels special and unhurried. The rival wins.

breakdown.label: Social
breakdown.detail: 'I planned something for you.' The rival wins.

cards.title: Researchers have mapped this for decades.
body: In 1991, marketing researchers Jagdish Sheth, Bruce Newman and Barbara Gross argued that people choose products based on several kinds of value, including functional, emotional and social.

In 2016, Bain & Company published a version in Harvard Business Review called the **Elements of Value**: 30 elements arranged in a pyramid, with functional needs at the base and emotional and social ones above.
The labels differ. The point is the same: price and features are only part of what customers weigh.

cards.title: The upper layers rest on the bottom one.
body: A candle on the dessert won't save a cold steak. Emotional and social value only work once the functional basics are solid.
Social value also depends on who is watching. What signals effort to one group looks showy to another.
And customers rarely say this out loud. They'll tell you about price and features. Watch what they choose, and when.

cards.title: Now it's an invoicing app.
body: Your app helps freelancers bill clients. It's faster and cheaper than the leader, but many trial users leave and say they'll stick with what they have.
In interviews, users mention two worries: looking amateur to clients, and not knowing if a payment slipped through. What do you build next?

options.text: Cut the price again and add more export formats
options.feedback: You deepen a lead you already have. Neither worry is about price or formats.

options.text: Polished invoice designs, plus clear alerts showing what's paid and what's late
options.feedback: Polished invoices answer how users look to clients. Clear alerts answer how they feel about money. Both are cheap to build compared to a price war.

options.text: Run ads saying you're twice as fast as the leader
options.feedback: Speed is real value, but it's functional. The ads may bring more trials without fixing why users leave.

cards.softwareNote: In software, social value often shows up in what other people see: the invoice a client opens, the report a boss reads, the link a teammate clicks.

cards.title: Customers buy what it does, how it feels and how it looks.
body: When you lose to a pricier rival, check all three layers before you cut prices or add features.
**Try it today:** pick your best-selling product. Write one sentence each for what it does, how it makes customers feel, and what it says about them to others. Which sentence was hardest?
